ad4408ba42:
This chapter is a first-principles look at the architecture decision that comes before any agent code. Should the control flow live in your program (a workflow) or in the model (an agent)?

It covers the five workflow patterns from Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) and the autonomous agent. It covers the arithmetic of error compounding that decides between them, manager/supervisor hierarchies, and subagents as a context-isolation mechanism. The story runs from workflow engines and enterprise integration patterns to multi-agent research systems. Implementations are in Python and Java.
c15468a654: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 02 builds the agent loop, the Claude Agent SDK harness and hooks. Chapter 03 covers memory, context management inside long runs, and the LangGraph / Strands / PydanticAI frameworks. This chapter decides which shape to build. Those chapters build it.
ee6066ae98:
Every LLM application sits somewhere on one axis: who decides what happens next, your code or the model. Put the decision in code (a workflow) whenever you can write the steps down in advance, and hand it to the model (an agent) only when the path depends on what the system discovers along the way and you can afford the extra cost, latency and error surface.

Hierarchies and subagents are not a third option; they are how you split an agentic system so that each model call has a small, focused context, a narrow tool set and a single job, with a coordinator that owns the communication.
76ae2f7d51:
The rest of the chapter unpacks those two sentences. The five workflow patterns are five ways of writing the control flow in code while still using a model for the steps:

  • run steps in sequence (chaining);
  • pick one of several paths (routing);
  • run steps side by side (parallelization);
  • let a model decide the subtasks but keep the shape fixed (orchestrator-workers);
  • loop until a judge is satisfied (evaluator-optimizer).

The autonomous agent is the limit case, where the model chooses every step. Each move along the axis buys flexibility. You pay for it in tokens, latency, predictability and testability. The exam is mostly about recognising which payment a scenario can afford.
0f07c147e0:
The CCDV-F guide states objective 1.1 in one line: workflow vs agent; manager/supervisor hierarchies; subagents. At 4.5% of a 53-item exam, that's two or three questions. But the concepts recur across Domain 1 and in scenario questions elsewhere (tools, context engineering, cost).

Typical stems give you a requirement with a tell:

  • "predictable", "auditable", "known steps" point to a workflow;
  • "unknown number of steps", "depends on what it finds" point to an agent;
  • "main context is filling up", "explore without polluting" point to a subagent;
  • "several specialists, one point of control" points to a supervisor.

Learning to read the tell is the goal.
84c02f6a5e: None of the vocabulary in this chapter is new. Chaining, routing, scatter-gather and supervisors are decades-old integration patterns, and you've almost certainly built most of them in Java. What changed is one kind of step. The model call can now make decisions that used to need a human or a hand-written rule. Tracing the lineage shows which parts of the old discipline still apply (most of them). It also shows which part is genuinely new: who holds the control flow.
020a68db46:
Business process engines (BPEL, later BPMN engines such as Activiti, Camunda and jBPM) formalised one idea. A long-running process is a graph of steps defined ahead of time. An engine executes it, persists state between steps, and handles compensation. It also gives operations staff a picture of where each instance is.

Telecom order management is a textbook example. An order for a new line moves through credit check, number reservation, SIM provisioning, activation and billing set-up. The engine knows which step every order is on.
48d5801f70:
In 2003, Hohpe and Woolf's Enterprise Integration Patterns catalogued the messaging shapes that connect such steps. Four of them map almost one-to-one onto this chapter:

  • Pipes and Filters: a fixed sequence of processing steps. That's prompt chaining.
  • Content-Based Router: inspect a message and send it to one of several channels. That's routing.
  • Scatter-Gather and Splitter/Aggregator: fan out to parallel workers and recombine. That's parallelization and orchestrator-workers.
  • Process Manager: a central component that decides the next step based on intermediate results. That's the supervisor.

If you've used Spring Integration or Apache Camel, you already know the shapes. Their weakness was the same as expert systems'. Each router predicate, each split rule, each next-step decision had to be written by a person.
a5accdac46:
The microservice era added a second axis that also carries over. In an orchestrated saga, a central orchestrator tells each service what to do and listens for replies. In a choreographed saga, services react to each other's events with no centre.

The industry settled on a rule of thumb that the multi-agent world has now rediscovered. Choreography is elegant for two or three participants and becomes undebuggable at ten, because nobody can say where a given business transaction is. Orchestration costs a central component. In return you get a single place to log, enforce timeouts and compensate. Section 12 makes the same argument for supervisors versus peer-to-peer agent handoffs.
fe35d236e0:
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) showed that a language model could interleave reasoning with actions in a loop. Native function calling in 2023 made that loop structured (chapter 02 covers the mechanics).

In spring 2023, open-source projects such as AutoGPT and BabyAGI wrapped the loop around a goal ("grow my business"). They let the model plan, spawn tasks and call tools with almost no constraints. They were very popular and rarely useful. Runs wandered, repeated themselves, burned tokens, and stopped only when a counter ran out.

The field didn't conclude that agents fail. It concluded that unconstrained autonomy on vague goals compounds small errors into useless results, and that most production value comes from much more structured designs.
1273f22a45:
Anthropic's engineering post "Building effective agents" (Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, December 2024) is the primary source for this objective. It summarised what Anthropic had seen across dozens of customer teams. The most successful implementations used simple, composable patterns rather than complex frameworks.

The post introduced the distinction this exam uses: workflows ("systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths") versus agents ("systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage"). It named the augmented LLM as the building block, and described five workflow patterns plus the autonomous agent.

Its advice is quoted almost verbatim in exam distractor analysis: find the simplest solution possible, and only increase complexity when needed. That might mean not building an agentic system at all.
b050cbc042:
In June 2025 Anthropic published how it built the multi-agent Research feature in Claude. A lead agent plans and spawns several subagents. They search in parallel, each with its own context window. The lead then synthesises their condensed findings.

The post reported large gains over a single agent on breadth-first research tasks. It was also candid about the cost: agents used roughly four times the tokens of a chat interaction, and multi-agent systems roughly fifteen times (figures from the post; check the source for exact numbers). It said multi-agent designs fit poorly when agents must share a lot of context or depend on each other step by step, as in most coding tasks.

In the same period, Claude Code shipped subagents. These are Markdown files with a name, description, tool list and system prompt, which the main agent can delegate to. The Claude Agent SDK exposed the same mechanism programmatically. Those two sources give the vocabulary for sections 12 and 13.
72d22eed65:
Strip away the terminology, and every LLM system is a program that calls a model one or more times. The architectural question is where the next-step decision is made.

In a workflow, your code holds the sequence of calls, the branches, the loops and their exit conditions. The model fills in each step: it extracts, classifies, drafts or judges. But it never chooses which step runs next. You can draw the workflow as a flowchart before the first request is sent, and every run follows a path through that chart.

In an agent, the program is a loop. It hands the model a goal and a set of tools and asks, each turn, "what now?". The model's answer (call this tool with these arguments, or stop) decides the next step. You can't draw the path in advance, because it depends on what the tools return.
c0f48562b1:
The distinction is about control flow, not about tools. A workflow step can call tools. A routing classifier can use a forced tool call to return a typed label. And an agent can be very small: a loop with two read-only tools is still an agent if the model decides whether to call the second one.

The test is simple. If you can write the full list of possible paths in a design document, you have a workflow. If the honest description is "it investigates until it figures it out", you have an agent.
bd7448cb59: Why does the exam test this distinction directly? Because it determines nearly every non-functional property of the system:
422aad237a: A Spring architect's intuition helps here. A workflow is a Spring Integration flow or a Camunda BPMN diagram where a few service tasks happen to call a model. An agent is closer to handing a junior engineer a runbook, a terminal with limited permissions, and the instruction "fix the ticket". You wouldn't do that for a process you could automate with a flowchart. And you wouldn't try to flowchart a novel production incident. The same judgement applies.
d2ed579327:
Every pattern in this chapter is built from one unit: a model call augmented with three things. With retrieval, your code puts relevant documents in the prompt. With tools, the model can request actions or lookups. With memory, state is carried across calls (covered in chapter 03).

Before reaching for any pattern, ask whether a single augmented call meets the requirement. A surprising share of production use cases are one well-prompted call with good context: summarising a call transcript, answering a plan question from a knowledge base, extracting fields from an invoice. Adding a chain or an agent makes them slower, more expensive and harder to test, with no gain in quality.
a492f79a93:
The augmentations are interfaces, and their quality matters more than the pattern around them. Retrieval that returns the wrong plan document makes every downstream step wrong. A tool with a vague description gets called at the wrong time (chapter 21).

Anthropic's guidance puts it this way: invest in the agent-computer interface the way you'd invest in a human-computer interface. In practice, a tool for "get line usage" takes a line number and returns a small, labelled JSON object. It doesn't return a dump of the billing database.
18dcc7a646: The companion example is the baseline every later example builds on. Retrieval puts the plan into the prompt, the model calls one tool, and the code returns the result.
c530100dd9: Notice that this already contains a tiny decision by the model: whether to call the tool. But the shape is fixed in code, with at most one tool round. That's still best described as an augmented call, not an agent. The line blurs at the edges, and the exam doesn't test the edge. It tests whether you reach for more machinery than the requirement needs.
3184665aa9: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a fixed sequence of steps. Each LLM call processes the output of the previous one. Your code can insert gates between steps: programmatic checks that decide whether the chain continues. It's the Pipes and Filters pattern, with model calls as filters.
a483a4bdda:
Why split a task that one call might do? Three reasons, in order of importance.

First, each call gets an easier job. Take "extract the region, service and ETA from this NOC note" and "write a friendly 160-character SMS from these three fields". Each is simpler and more reliable than "turn this NOC note into an SMS", because the model doesn't have to juggle extraction accuracy and tone at once.

Second, gates catch errors at the boundary, where they're cheap to detect. They catch them before they become a wrong message to a million customers.

Third, each step can use a different model and prompt: extraction on a small fast model, customer-facing writing on a stronger one.

You trade latency (calls are sequential) for accuracy and control.
d6c3505c0c: When the extraction drops the ETA, gate 1 raises and step 2 never runs. The test asserts exactly that: one call made, no SMS produced. That's what gates buy you: "a failure at step k costs k calls and produces no output".
8be869030a:
The most common chaining bug is to pipe raw output from one call into the next prompt with no check. Models are good at producing plausible text from whatever they're given. So a malformed or incomplete intermediate result doesn't cause an error. It causes a confident wrong answer two steps later.

In the companion's broken version, step 1 returns prose instead of JSON, and no ETA. Step 2 cheerfully writes "Your service in Dallas is restored". Nothing crashed. The customer got false information.
95725ef10b:
Three details in the fix are worth remembering.

  • The retry carries the specific error and the previous output, so the model can correct rather than guess again.
  • The prompt now gives an explicit value for missing information ("unknown"). That removes the pressure to invent an ETA. Retries can't recover information that isn't in the source.
  • When retries are exhausted, the chain raises instead of passing on whatever it has, so the caller can route to a human.

In production you'd usually get JSON via a forced tool call or structured outputs (chapter 18), so syntax errors disappear. The semantic gate (is the ETA present and plausible?) is still your job.
9cbac2e288:
When to use chaining: the task splits cleanly into fixed subtasks, each subtask is easier than the whole, and you can check the intermediate result. Typical uses: extract then transform then format; draft an outline, check it against rules, then write; generate, then translate.

When not to: when the steps aren't known ahead of time (that's an orchestrator or agent). Or when latency matters more than the accuracy gain, since every link adds a full round trip.
d68e3bdaf9:
Routing classifies an input once and sends it to one of several specialised follow-up paths. It's the Content-Based Router with a model as the predicate.

The benefit is separation of concerns. Without routing, one prompt has to handle billing questions, outage reports, device troubleshooting and fraud-sensitive port-out requests. Optimising that prompt for one category tends to hurt the others.

With routing, each path gets its own system prompt, its own tools, its own guardrails and, importantly for cost, its own model. Simple billing FAQs go to the cheapest tier. Port-out requests carry SIM-swap fraud risk, so they go to the strongest model with strict instructions.
fd70e67ff1: Routing can be done by a model or by conventional code (keyword rules, a trained classifier, the IVR menu choice). Use a model when categories are expressed in natural language with many phrasings. Use code when a field already tells you the answer. Don't pay for an LLM call to read a dropdown value.
c4fb377b6d:
Three design rules turn a routing demo into a routing system.

  • Make the classifier output typed. Force a tool call whose input schema has an enum of categories, so you never parse "I think this is probably billing".
  • Include an "other" category and a confidence. Send low-confidence or "other" results to a safe default: a general agent, or a human queue.
  • Keep the classifier on a cheap model. It runs on every request, so it dominates call volume.
a7397d4de7: A caution about the confidence number. A model's self-reported confidence is a weak signal, and it isn't calibrated in the statistical sense. Treat it as one input to the fallback rule. Measure how often each confidence band is right on a labelled sample, and set the threshold from that data, not from intuition.
7699999bee:
Routing makes one decision up front. Take a ticket that says "my bill went up $40 and my phone has had no signal since Tuesday". It contains two issues, and a single-label router sends it down one path. This is the same failure that plagued intent-classifier chatbots in the 2010s.

There are three remedies, in increasing order of flexibility:

  • allow a multi-label classifier and run the matching handlers in parallel (routing plus sectioning);
  • split the input into issues first (a chaining step) and route each;
  • recognise that the case needs an agent that can investigate both and connect them. Maybe the roaming charge and the signal loss are the same trip abroad.

The exam likes this scenario because adding more categories ("billing+device") is the tempting wrong answer. It grows the tree combinatorially.
bbdf9cf486: Parallelization runs several LLM calls at the same time and combines their outputs in code. It comes in two variants, which solve different problems:
f533424ca6: Sectioning: split a task into independent subtasks and run them concurrently. The point is latency, since total time is the slowest call and not the sum. It's also focus, since each call handles one aspect. In EIP terms, this is Scatter-Gather.
fdf684fa4a: Voting: run the same task several times, often with varied prompts, and aggregate the answers. The point is confidence. Several independent looks catch errors a single look misses. You can tune the aggregation threshold to trade false positives against false negatives.
418432980a:
Anthropic's post calls out sectioning a guardrail this way. One model instance screens the request while another answers it. That tends to work better than asking one call to do both, because each has a single clear job.

The trade-off is cost: you pay for the answer even when the guard blocks it. There's also a subtle security point. The blocked answer must never reach the user, or a log the user can see. Because code makes the decision to release the answer, that property is easy to guarantee and test.
47f9d83f10:
Why vary the prompts? Votes are only useful if their errors are somewhat independent. Three identical calls at low temperature tend to make the same mistake three times. Different framings, or different emphasis on the evidence, decorrelate them.

The threshold is a business decision. For fraud you might flag on one vote of three: catch more, review more. For an automated content takedown you might require all three. Voting multiplies cost by N, so reserve it for decisions where a miss is expensive.
fffbe52060:
Broken vs fixed. The common sectioning bug is to parallelise steps that aren't independent. For example, you draft the customer reply in parallel with the account lookup it depends on. The draft then has to guess the account state. If step B reads step A's output, it's a chain, not a section.

The common voting bug is aggregating in a model ("here are three answers, which is right?"). That reintroduces a single point of judgement and hides the tally. Aggregate in code, where the rule is visible and testable.
9dc2d61bc6:
In orchestrator-workers, a central LLM (the orchestrator) looks at the input and decides what subtasks are needed. It delegates each one to a worker LLM call. A synthesis step then combines the results.

It looks like sectioning, and the difference is the key exam point. In sectioning, you wrote the list of subtasks. In orchestrator-workers, the model writes it, at run time, because it depends on the input. "Which files does this rate-plan migration touch?" can't be answered before reading the code. So the list of per-file or per-service tasks can't be hard-coded.
36bc6c3c07: Anthropic's taxonomy still classes it as a workflow, because the shape is fixed: plan, fan out, gather, synthesise, done. The orchestrator decides what the workers do. It doesn't decide whether to loop, or which phase comes next. You get most of the flexibility of an agent for decomposable problems, while keeping a bounded number of calls and a predictable structure. The Splitter/Aggregator from EIP is the ancestor. The novelty is that the splitter is a model.
6777b5adc7:
Four decisions in this code carry over to every orchestrator you build.

  • The plan is a forced tool call with a schema, so data drives the fan-out, not parsed prose.
  • The number of workers is capped in code (max_workers). A model asked to decompose can over-decompose, and an uncapped fan-out is an uncapped bill.
  • Each worker receives only its brief, so the brief must be self-contained. Section 13 explains why this is the most common failure.
  • Workers return structured results, so the synthesis step merges facts, not essays.

Workers can run on a cheaper model than the orchestrator, because each has a narrow job. The orchestrator and synthesiser need judgement across the whole problem, so they get the stronger model.
0f249f004f:
When to use: the work splits into independent pieces, but which pieces depends on the input. Examples are multi-file code changes, research across an unknown set of sources, and auditing a variable set of network regions.

When not to: when pieces depend heavily on each other (a worker needs another worker's output mid-task), because workers can't talk to each other in this shape. Or when the subtasks are fixed. That's plain sectioning, and it's cheaper.
f48ce00097:
In evaluator-optimizer, one LLM call generates a response. Another evaluates it against explicit criteria and returns feedback. The generator revises, and the loop repeats until the evaluator passes it or a round budget runs out. It mirrors how a writer works with an editor.

Two conditions make it worth the cost, and Anthropic's post states both. There are clear evaluation criteria. And iteration measurably improves the result: a human giving feedback would make it better, and a model can give similar feedback.

Customer apology messages with a compliance rubric qualify. So do translations that must preserve terminology, and SQL that must pass a linter and a test query. "Make it more engaging" doesn't. Without crisp criteria the evaluator has nothing reliable to check, and the loop wanders.
4ddd8a4eed:
Why a separate evaluator call, rather than asking the generator to "check your work"? A model reviewing its own output in the same context tends to accept its own reasoning. The reasoning that produced the draft is sitting right there, and it looks convincing. A fresh call that sees only the rubric and the draft has no such anchor.

It's the same principle as an independent code reviewer. The exam reuses it for code review scenarios: the same Claude session is worse at reviewing changes it just made.
11ee2b5e97:
Two more design points.

Wherever a criterion can be checked by code (length, required phrase, JSON validity, a test suite), check it in code and feed the failure to the generator. Use the model evaluator only for criteria code can't judge, such as tone or faithfulness to source.

And the loop needs a round budget with escalation. Without a budget, a generator and evaluator that disagree about an ambiguous criterion will ping-pong forever. With a budget that silently returns the last draft, you ship something the evaluator rejected. Neither is acceptable for a customer-facing message.
5ae9f16683: An agent, in the exam's sense, is a model using tools in a loop based on environmental feedback. It receives a goal, picks an action, observes the result, and picks the next action. It keeps going until it decides it's done or a limit stops it. Chapter 02 builds that loop in detail (the stop_reason protocol, tool-result pairing, the Agent SDK). Here the question is architectural: when is an agent the right shape?
63ed8217f4:
Anthropic's guidance gives the conditions. The problem is open-ended, and the number of steps can't be predicted. You can't hard-code a fixed path. And you can trust the model's decisions enough to let it act in that environment. The canonical examples are coding agents (which files to read and change depends on what the code says) and investigation tasks.

A telecom example: "No service on 555-0101 since this morning." The cause might be an account suspension, a failed eSIM download after a SIM change, a tower outage, a device fault, or two of these at once. Each finding changes what to check next.

A workflow that tries to cover this becomes a decision tree with dozens of branches, and it still misses combinations. An agent with read tools for account, device and network, plus one carefully guarded action tool, handles the case in three steps.
ebc2d3ced5:
In the scripted run, the model checks account and device in parallel. It sees "eSIM state: DOWNLOAD_FAILED" next to "SIM changed 1h ago", re-pushes the eSIM, and explains. Nobody wrote "if SIM changed recently and eSIM failed, resend".

Deploy the same code with allowed set to the read-only tools, and it refuses the action with an is_error result. The model escalates instead. That split is the core of safe agent design: the model decides what to try; code decides what is allowed.
882f51fa91:
Agents fail in a way workflows mostly don't, and a little arithmetic shows why. Suppose each step of a process is right with probability p, independently. A process of n steps with no checks is right end to end with probability pn. At 95% per step, 10 steps give about 60%, and 25 steps give about 28%.

Agents take more steps than workflows. And each step's input includes the outputs of earlier steps. So an early mistake, such as reading the wrong account, poisons everything after it.
85370c266d:
Two things change the arithmetic.

The first lever: Checks with recovery. If a failed step is detected with probability c and retried, the effective per-step success becomes p + (1 - p)·c·p. With p = 0.95 and c = 0.9, a 10-step process goes from 60% to about 93%.

Workflows get this from gates. Agents get it from ground truth from the environment: a tool result that says the eSIM is still failing, or a test suite that fails. That ground truth lets the model notice and correct its own mistakes. It's why agents work best where the environment gives clear feedback (code with tests, systems with observable state). They work worst where it doesn't (open-ended writing, judgement calls with no check).

The second lever is fewer steps. A workflow that does in three calls what an agent does in twelve has less room to compound.
f5dd79e83f:
The practical consequences are what the exam tests. Agents need:

  • budgets (step, token, time) as circuit breakers that escalate when tripped;
  • sandboxed, least-privilege tools, because they'll sometimes try the wrong action;
  • human checkpoints before irreversible actions;
  • extensive testing in a sandbox before production.

And agents are the most expensive shape. The history is resent every turn, so cost grows faster than the number of steps. The companion's cost model (example 16) puts an 8-turn agent at about 14 times a single call, and a lead with three subagents at about 50 times, with placeholder prices. When the requirement says "cost-sensitive, high volume, well-defined", an agent is almost never the answer.
61f1df3850: The selection logic fits in a short sequence of questions, asked from the simple end of the spectrum. The companion turns it into code (15_choose_pattern.py) with exam-style cases. It's a good way to test your own reading of a scenario.
c0c5af3ac6:
Real systems compose patterns. A contact-centre assistant might:

  • route each ticket (pattern 2);
  • send billing tickets down a three-step chain (pattern 1);
  • send "no service" tickets to an agent (section 10) whose outage check fans out to regions in parallel (pattern 3);
  • pass every outbound customer message through an evaluator with a compliance rubric (pattern 5).

The exam rarely asks you to name a composite. It asks which single change best addresses the stated problem. Read the problem and find the one property that's failing: predictability, latency, accuracy, coverage of unforeseen cases, or context size. Then pick the pattern that fixes exactly that.
e415154171: Once a single agent has too many responsibilities, the usual next step is to split it into several agents with narrower roles. The question is how they relate. Three topologies cover nearly every design you'll meet. They map directly onto the orchestration-versus-choreography debate from microservices.
87c095b24f:
A supervisor (also called manager, coordinator, orchestrator or lead agent) is an agent whose tools are mostly "delegate to specialist X". It reads the request and decides which specialists to involve. It writes a brief for each, receives their results, and composes the answer. Specialists don't talk to each other; everything passes through the hub.

That gives four properties that matter in production and on the exam:

  • a single place to log every delegation and result (observability);
  • a single place to enforce policy (which specialist may be called for which customer, budgets);
  • a single place to stop the run;
  • specialists with narrow tool sets. The billing specialist has invoice tools only, so it can't mistakenly touch network configuration.
e768159259:
Look at the tool description: "Include every fact it needs; it cannot see this conversation." Tool descriptions are how the supervisor learns to delegate, so the delegation contract belongs there.

In the run, the supervisor sends two briefs in one turn (billing and network), each self-contained. The audit log shows exactly what each specialist was asked and what it answered. That log is what you show an operations team when a customer disputes the answer.
aafe1d2aab:
Sometimes the number of specialists grows past what one supervisor can choose between reliably. Tool-selection accuracy drops as the tool list grows (chapter 21). Then you nest supervisors: a top-level manager delegates to team leads, and each lead supervises its own specialists.

This is an org chart, with the same benefits and the same costs. Each lead has a manageable span. But there are more hops, more latency, and more places for information to get lost in summaries. Use it when the role set is genuinely large, not as a default.
e062309081:
In a handoff design (sometimes called a swarm), agents transfer control directly. The triage agent hands the conversation to the billing agent, which may hand it to the network agent. Some frameworks offer this as a primitive. It works for small, linear flows where each agent fully owns the conversation while active, much like transferring a phone call between departments.

Its weaknesses are the choreography weaknesses. No single component knows the overall state. Loops between agents are hard to detect. Policy has to be enforced in every agent. For exam questions that mention observability, governance, auditability or consistent policy enforcement, the hub-and-spoke supervisor is the expected answer.
c66bdd31ff: A subagent is an agent that another agent invokes to do a bounded piece of work. It runs in its own, separate context window and returns only its final result. Specialists in a supervisor design are subagents. So are the workers in a research fan-out, and so are the subagents you define in Claude Code. The mechanics differ by platform, but the architectural idea is the same everywhere. It's mostly about context, not about intelligence.
fabf564877:
Start from the constraint. An agent's context window holds everything it has seen in the run: system prompt, tool definitions, every tool call and every tool result. Investigation work is verbose.

Say the agent reads a 2,500-line radio-access log to find which cells degraded. That puts tens of thousands of tokens into the window, and they stay there for every later turn. They cost money, add latency, and dilute the model's attention on what matters (chapter 16 calls this context rot). The lead agent needed one sentence from that log.

A subagent lets the reading happen in a disposable context. The subagent reads the log and writes a three-sentence summary. Then its whole context is discarded. Only the summary enters the lead's window.
c28348abba: Least privilege. Each subagent gets only the tools its job needs. A log analyst gets read and search, not write or deploy. A mistake in one can't use another's permissions.
e4c987c809:
Isolation moves tokens; it doesn't delete them. The companion's measurement makes this concrete. With a subagent, the lead's context grows by about 60 tokens instead of about 30,000. But the subagent still spent about 30,000 tokens reading the log. Total spend is the same or higher, with an extra system prompt and an extra summarisation call. What improved is the lead's context quality, and the lead's cost on every later turn.

So multi-agent systems are more expensive overall, as Anthropic's research post states directly. They also lose information at every handoff. The summary is a lossy compression, and if the lead later needs a detail the subagent didn't report, it has to ask again. And they're harder to debug, because the reasoning is spread across several transcripts.
febe04a0cc: A subagent does not inherit the parent's conversation. It sees its own system prompt, its tools, and whatever the parent put in the delegation brief. The parent may have spent twenty turns with the customer, learning the account number, the billing period, and what's been ruled out. All of that is invisible unless the brief includes it. The bug looks like this:
1606b541b4:
A good brief has five parts. They're worth memorising, because they also make a good tool description for a delegation tool:

  • the goal: the outcome, not a procedure;
  • the facts the subagent needs: identifiers, prior findings, what has been ruled out;
  • the constraints: scope, permissions, what not to do;
  • the output format: structured, with evidence or sources so the lead can check claims;
  • the done criteria: when to stop, and what to say if the task can't be completed.

Anthropic's research-system write-up reports exactly this failure class in early versions. Vague delegation led subagents to duplicate each other's work or interpret the task differently. Detailed task descriptions with objectives, output formats, tool guidance and boundaries fixed it.
13d5913553: For independent subtasks, the lead should emit several delegation tool calls in a single response. The harness runs them concurrently. It returns all the results together in the next user message, each tied to its tool_use_id. Serialising them (delegate, wait, delegate, wait) gives the same answer at several times the latency.
75a0e1c401: You can build subagents by hand with the Messages API, as the examples do. A subagent is just a separate messages.create loop with its own system prompt and tools, called from a tool handler in the parent. Anthropic's agent products package the same idea. Chapter 02 covers the SDK wiring and chapter 11 the Claude Code operation, so here is only the shape.
d99c11f1e8:
In Claude Code, a file like this in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (personal) defines a subagent. The main agent reads the description when deciding whether to delegate, so it should say when to use it. tools restricts what it may do. model can pick a cheaper tier. Claude Code also ships built-in subagents, such as a read-only Explore agent for codebase search (check the docs for the current list).

In the Claude Agent SDK, the equivalent is an agents mapping of names to AgentDefinition(description=..., prompt=..., tools=[...], model=...) in ClaudeAgentOptions. The parent invokes subagents through the SDK's delegation tool, historically named Task. That tool must be in the parent's allowed tools (newer releases may name it differently; check the docs).

Two platform rules matter for design. The subagent receives only the prompt the parent writes for it. And Claude Code subagents can't spawn further subagents, so you must build deep hierarchies in your own orchestration code (check the docs for current limits).
ef33698ca8: Every failure mode below has been reported in practice, and each has a matching exam distractor. Most are failures of decomposition or communication, not of model capability.
7d5ab85a7a: Notice how many fixes are "put the decision in code": caps, partitioning, required fields, budgets, the hub. It's the principle from section 03, applied one level up. A multi-agent system works when the overall structure is deliberate, and only the parts that need judgement are left to the models.
5df5b7de14: Nothing in these patterns is Python-specific. On the JVM the shapes are the ones you already use. The only new component is a client that calls the Messages API. Anthropic publishes an official Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java; check the docs for current coordinates and builder method names). To keep the patterns independent of SDK details, the sketches below program against a small interface. You'd implement it with that SDK or with Spring's RestClient.
b00da5173a:
Two Spring-specific notes.

First, injecting Map<String, TicketHandler> gives you the routing table for free from bean names. That keeps routes declarative and testable. It's the same trick you'd use for a strategy pattern.

Second, the voting code shows a decision the Python version leaves implicit: what happens when one vote times out. For a fraud check, failing closed (count the missing vote as suspicious) is the defensible default. For a content-generation vote you might drop it. Decide explicitly.

On Java 21 you can replace the executor with virtual threads, since these calls spend nearly all their time waiting on the network.
495d98e9bc:
For orchestrator-workers and supervisors, the mapping is to a Process Manager: a component that holds per-request state and decides the next step. A supervisor is a Process Manager whose next-step decision comes from a model. So the Java implementation is the agent loop from chapter 02, with delegation tools whose handlers call other Llm-backed services.

If your organisation already runs Camunda or Temporal, the workflow patterns fit naturally as service tasks or activities. That gives you persistence, retries and visibility for free. An agent loop fits as a single long-running activity with heartbeats.
5a8733e0bb:
Workflow patterns have a large deterministic part: gates, routing tables, thresholds, round budgets, fan-out caps, result pairing. Unit-test that part like any other code, without calling a model.

The companion's fake_client.py mimics the Messages API response shape (content blocks with type, stop_reason, usage) and returns scripted replies. It serves them either in order or from a responder function that inspects the request. You need the responder for parallel calls, whose order isn't fixed. It also records a snapshot of every request, so tests can assert on what was sent.
eb6a2661bd:
Be clear about what these tests prove. They prove your control flow is right. A low-confidence label goes to the human queue. A failed gate stops the chain. A spent budget escalates. Specialists never receive the supervisor's history (example 11 asserts this).

They prove nothing about whether the real model classifies tickets well or writes good apologies. That needs evaluation against the real model on a labelled set, covered in chapter 12. A sound test strategy has both: fast deterministic tests on every commit, and slower model evals on prompt or model changes.
884d672c54: CCDV-F items give a short scenario and four options. For 1.1, the wrong options are usually real techniques applied to the wrong problem: an agent where a workflow fits, a bigger model where the context is the problem, more categories where the input is multi-issue. Work each one before reading the reasoning.
7bff393d93:
The steps are fixed and known, and the requirement stresses consistency and auditability. That's the definition of a workflow. B puts the order in code and the disclosure check in a deterministic gate, and it logs at known points.

A hands the order to the model and then asks it to behave like a workflow. That's probabilistic and harder to audit. C removes the check between extraction and generation. D adds cost and complexity for flexibility the task doesn't need.
79278d9b32:
Single-label routing makes one decision up front, so multi-issue input is its blind spot. And the possible link between issues needs investigation that depends on findings. C is model-driven: it can check both issues and relate them.

A grows the category set combinatorially and still can't connect findings. B keeps one label per ticket. D wastes calls, produces contradictory text, and still can't connect the two issues. A multi-label router with parallel handlers would partly help, but not with the link. That's why C is best here.
64756033fc:
The problem is context pollution. Verbose tool output fills the lead's window and dilutes attention on the important facts. B isolates the verbose work in disposable subagent contexts and returns only conclusions. It also gives least privilege.

A gives more room for the same pollution: attention and latency problems persist, and cost rises. C asks the model to overcome a structural issue with an instruction. D limits capability arbitrarily and may miss the root cause. (Compaction and tool-result clearing, chapter 03 and 16, are complementary fixes.)
5218b8902f:
Subagents start with an empty conversation. They see their own system prompt, their tools and the brief. B is the documented behaviour, and the fix: self-contained briefs with goal, facts, constraints, format and done criteria, plus a delegation tool description that says so.

A misdiagnoses the cause. C would undo the isolation, which is the reason to use subagents in the first place. D breaks the hub-and-spoke design and annoys the customer.
e82626189f:
The symptoms are the classic choreography problems: no central view, policy enforced in many places, cycles. A hub-and-spoke supervisor gives one place to log, enforce and stop.

A patches one symptom with a probabilistic instruction. C fixes traceability, but it recreates the too-many-tools and context problems that motivated specialists, and it loses least privilege. D makes the loop longer.
febf8ad561:
Clear criteria, and iteration that helps: that's evaluator-optimizer. B also checks in code what code can check. It uses a separate evaluator to avoid self-review bias, and it has a round budget with escalation.

A is self-review in the same context. C is voting with a meaningless aggregator. D adds autonomy the fixed task doesn't need.
98ed51986d: In 04_routing.py, add a multi-issue ticket ("bill went up and no signal"). Change the route tool to return a list of categories, and run the matching handlers with asyncio.gather. What does the fallback rule become?
8297652cd4: In 12_subagent_context_isolation.py, change the log to 20,000 lines. Compute the lead's input tokens over a 10-turn run in both designs (history is resent each turn). At what log size does the subagent design become cheaper in total, and not just cleaner?
9bffbd249e: Run 15_choose_pattern.py. Then add three scenarios of your own from your work (for example port-in validation, outage notification, network config review). Check that the heuristic agrees with your judgement. Where it doesn't, decide which one is wrong.
2b512d7e2a: Done when: you can name the pattern for any scenario in under ten seconds and say what property it buys. You can explain why a subagent saves the lead's context but not total tokens. And you can write a self-contained delegation brief from memory (goal, facts, constraints, output, done).
